questions: How can scientific pretence and resistance to evidence be assessed without turning warning signs into automatic verdicts?

Philosophical discussions on the characterization of pseudoscience have usually focused on the missing scientific quality of pseudoscience (rather than on its attempt to mimic science).

In 1933, Karl Popper published a short text in which he introduced the German term “Abgrenzungsproblem” (later translated as “demarcation problem”) for the identification of claims that should not be classified as scientific.

In an essay published in 1962, he specified his purpose as “drawing a line of demarcation between those statements and systems of statements which could be properly described as belonging to empirical science, and others which might, perhaps, be described as ‘pseudo-scientific’ or (in certain contexts) as ‘metaphysical’, or which belonged, perhaps, to pure logic or to pure mathematics” (Popper 1962, 255).
This is a different task than that of providing a complete definition of pseudoscience, and also a different task than that of providing a complete definition of science (Debray 2023).

The use of the demarcation metaphor for the identification of pseudoscience can therefore give the impression that the task of determining whether a particular claim is pseudoscientific or not can be performed without any specialized knowledge in the subject matter (Hansson 2025).
Karl Popper described the demarcation problem as the “key to most of the fundamental problems in the philosophy of science” (Popper 1962, 42).
